body.text: The United States’ 2026 midterm elections delivered a divided government. Democrats won the House of Representative decisively – roughly 30 seats flipped, in all favor of Democrats – and captured the Senate, gaining seven seats across states like Texas, North Carolina, Ohio, and Maine. Two weeks from now, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump will meet in Shenzhen on the margins of APEC –first encounter since the midterm results and the last leaders’ meeting of the year.

In Washington, the dominant reading of the past year is that the trade war was overplayed and is now being walked back. Similarly, Beijing tends to view renewed engagement as a sign that China has successfully endured U.S. pressure. In May we warned against precisely this habit – treating engagement after escalation as a concession.

The midterms add another complication, as the U.S. political mood has turned sharply against Trump. But those results don’t change the topics that should lead the agenda for the Trump-Xi summit in Shenzhen.

In October, we argued that Trump and Xi need to talk about the growing signs of an AI bubble. The seven U.S. companies at the center of the AI buildout spent $657 billion on capital expenditure from the last quarter of 2025 through the third quarter of 2026. None of them has projected a spending cut in the next year.

Yet the stock market’s attention has shifted from earnings to spending. Oracle, whose cloud backlog reached $638 billion, up 363 percent, saw its shares fall by half over 12 months as its free cash flow went to negative $23.7 billion. Amazon’s trailing free cash flow collapsed 95 percent even as it raised capex to roughly $220 billion; Alphabet reported its first negative free-cash-flow quarter. Profits may be high, but markets are increasingly worried about the direction of capital spending.

Consider the industry’s most aggressive builder. In May, Elon Musk dissolved xAI as a standalone company and folded it into SpaceXAI; on the same day, SpaceX announced it was renting the entire Colossus 1 cluster – some 220,000 GPUs – to Anthropic, the maker of Claude. In September, Musk said Colossus 2, the gigawatt-scale site in Memphis, would more than double its Nvidia chip count before year-end. The speed was remarkable: the original cluster was reportedly built in 122 days. But the bill is just as eye-catching. The new data center reportedly sparked $430 million in contractor liens and a $30 million wrongful-death lawsuit.

Concern about data centers was a campaign issue in the U.S. midterms. From Wall Street to Main Street, questions are growing about the speed and scale of the AI buildout. The industry’s future from here will be determined by quarterly earnings calls, power procurement, and pending legal battles – not by firms’ strategy documents.

China’s AI buildout, meanwhile, is being determined by industrial planning and by a pricing war that has pushed frontier-model API prices to roughly a tenth of Western levels. But Beijing must not interpret the growing caution in the United States as victory by default. Litigation and permit battles will ultimately produce hardened, legitimate infrastructure. And China’s own AI sector is not exempt from the cash flow issue – the leading cloud providers turned cash-negative this year.
Both China and the U.S. must eventually answer the same question: not whose models are stronger, but whose AI buildout can actually pay for itself.
What does this mean for the Trump-Xi summit in Shenzhen?

First, the trade agenda is becoming more urgent, not less. In September, Trump and Xi agreed to start a Board of Trade that would work on reciprocal tariff reductions. Now comes implementation: what tariffs are cut, on what schedule, and how compliance is verified. Trump is facing an opposition Congress, elected on the back of economic discontent. Movement on tariffs lets him claim progress on lowering prices. For Beijing, predictability is the prize. The new Board of Trade should take steps small enough to survive a hostile Congress, but big enough to matter in aggregate.

Second, China and the United States need to consider AI guardrails in terms of the market significance, not just diplomatic significance. The second round of the official AI dialogue is due before the end of November, with a chance to make progress on another deliverable from the September summit: a new incident-communication channel. Markets now price political risk in real time, and they will read the Shenzhen summit as a risk-management event. A visible reaffirmation that the government are moving to address AI risks would drain the urgency from de-coupling pressure in the new Congress.

Third, China-U.S. crisis management belongs at the top of the agenda. The incoming Congress shares a bipartisan skepticism of Beijing, and could pursue legislation on sensitive bilateral issues like Taiwan. In Shenzhen, Trump and Xi can preemptively strengthen the military communication lines and incident channels that prevent accidents from spiralling into conflict. Beijing can afford patience but not surprises. Washington, heading into an era of divided government, should want the same insurance against catastrophe.

After the midterms, both Beijing and Washington need to avoid misinterpreting the state of the relationship. The trade war of 2025 was not won or lost. Instead, its costs were built into the operating environment of both economies. The question the incoming U.S. Congress should ask is not who “won” but what changed – and whether those changes are reversible.

Shenzhen comes as a crucial moment. Politics in Washington is about to accelerate. With congressional hearings expected to start in January, Trump needs deliverables more than ever. The 2028 presidential campaign, in some ways, has is already underway. Things are also moving quickly in the AI sector, as massive spending sprees run up against the reality of profit margins.

Trump and Xi cannot fully control either of these dynamics. They can, however, keep these factors from forcing China-U.S. relations onto a collision course – through small, reversible deliverables that let both sides show something at home, and through guardrails strong enough to survive opposition control of the U.S. legislature.
The September summit produced a to-do list. The summit in Shenzhen will test whether U.S. politics is going to derail those outcomes.
